core: What the criminal-process amendments regulate: government conduct during investigation, charging, trial, and punishment, rather than the definition of offenses
Fourth Amendment text and structure: the reasonableness clause and the warrant clause, and what the text does and does not require
Fifth Amendment: grand jury, double jeopardy, self-incrimination and the Miranda warnings, due process, and the takings clause identified as outside criminal procedure
Sixth Amendment: speedy and public trial, impartial jury, notice, confrontation, compulsory process, and assistance of counsel, with Gideon, Argersinger, and Strickland
Eighth Amendment: excessive bail, excessive fines, cruel and unusual punishments
Fourteenth Amendment due process and equal protection, and selective incorporation as the mechanism applying most Bill of Rights guarantees to the states

The exclusionary rule: Weeks, Silverthorne, Mapp; and its limits: good faith (Leon), inevitable discovery (Nix), independent source (Silverthorne/Nix), attenuation (Wong Sun), and Herring's negligence line
The unresolved debate over the exclusionary rule's costs and benefits, presented from the opinions themselves without taking a side
The separation of a right from its remedy
supporting: Barron v. Baltimore as the pre-incorporation baseline
Hurtado v. California and the grand jury clause as a standing non-incorporation example
McDonald v. Chicago's 2010 catalogue of unincorporated guarantees, read against Timbs (2019)
Duncan v. Louisiana on the criminal jury and the serious-offense line
Crawford v. Washington on testimonial statements under the Confrontation Clause
In re Winship giving due process concrete content at trial through the reasonable-doubt standard

The mechanics of arrest, initial appearance, preliminary hearing, and trial procedure, owned by arrest-through-trial and trial-and-sentencing
Bail-setting practice, release conditions, and pretrial detention policy, owned by bail-and-pretrial-procedure
Plea bargaining doctrine, owned by plea-bargaining
The criminal versus civil standards-of-proof comparison, owned by the merged criminal-law-versus-civil-law topic

claims.claim: The Fourth Amendment secures persons, houses, papers, and effects against unreasonable searches and seizures, and separately provides that no warrants shall issue but upon probable cause, supported by oath or affirmation, and particularly describing the place to be searched and the persons or things to be seized.

The Fifth Amendment contains five distinct guarantees: grand jury presentment or indictment for capital or otherwise infamous crimes (with an armed-forces and militia exception), double jeopardy, the privilege against compelled self-incrimination, due process, and just compensation for takings; only the first four bear on criminal procedure.

The Sixth Amendment applies 'in all criminal prosecutions' and lists a speedy and public trial, an impartial jury of the state and district of the crime, notice of the nature and cause of the accusation, confrontation with adverse witnesses, compulsory process for defense witnesses, and the assistance of counsel.
The Eighth Amendment in a single sentence forbids excessive bail, excessive fines, and cruel and unusual punishments.

The Fourteenth Amendment was passed by Congress on June 13, 1866 and ratified on July 9, 1868; its Section 1 forbids any state to deprive a person of life, liberty, or property without due process of law, or to deny any person within its jurisdiction the equal protection of the laws.

Barron v. Baltimore, 32 U.S. (7 Pet.) 243 (1833), held that the Fifth Amendment's just-compensation provision is solely a limitation on the federal government and does not apply to state legislation, reasoning that the Constitution was ordained by the people for their own government rather than for the governments of individual states. Opinion by Chief Justice Marshall.

Hurtado v. California, 110 U.S. 516 (1884), decided March 3, 1884, held that Fourteenth Amendment due process does not necessarily require grand jury indictment in a state prosecution for murder, so a California conviction on an information filed after a magistrate's examination was valid. Opinion by Justice Matthews.

As of 2010 the Supreme Court itself catalogued the guarantees not fully incorporated against the states as the Third Amendment quartering protection, the Fifth Amendment grand jury indictment requirement, the Seventh Amendment civil jury right, and the Eighth Amendment excessive fines prohibition; the same footnote records that the excessive bail prohibition's application to the states had only been assumed, in Schilb v. Kuebel, 404 U.S. 357 (1971).

Timbs v. Indiana, decided February 20, 2019, held the Eighth Amendment's Excessive Fines Clause is an incorporated protection applicable to the states through the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause; the incorporation test asks whether a protection is fundamental to our scheme of ordered liberty or deeply rooted in this Nation's history and tradition, and once incorporated there is no daylight between the federal and state conduct it governs. Opinion by Justice Ginsburg; no Justice dissented from the judgment.
The Timbs facts involved Indiana's attempt to forfeit a Land Rover Timbs had purchased for $42,000 with insurance proceeds, against a maximum $10,000 monetary fine assessable for his drug conviction.

Gideon v. Wainwright, decided March 18, 1963, held that an indigent defendant's right to the assistance of counsel at a criminal trial is a fundamental right essential to a fair trial and that conviction without counsel violated the Fourteenth Amendment, overruling Betts v. Brady, 316 U.S. 455. Opinion by Justice Black; no dissents.

Argersinger v. Hamlin, decided June 12, 1972, held that the right to appointed counsel is not governed by the classification of the offense or by whether a jury trial is required, and that absent a knowing and intelligent waiver no person may be imprisoned unless represented by counsel at trial. Opinion by Justice Douglas.

Strickland v. Washington, decided May 14, 1984, requires a defendant claiming ineffective assistance to show both that counsel's representation fell below an objective standard of reasonableness, judged with a strong presumption that counsel's conduct fell within the wide range of reasonable professional assistance, and that the deficiency prejudiced the defense, meaning a reasonable probability - one sufficient to undermine confidence in the outcome - that the result would have been different. Opinion by Justice O'Connor.

Duncan v. Louisiana, decided May 20, 1968, held that because trial by jury in criminal cases is fundamental to the American scheme of justice the Fourteenth Amendment guarantees jury trial in state cases that would come within the Sixth Amendment guarantee if tried federally, and that a crime punishable by two years in prison is serious - while expressly declining to define the petty-serious boundary. Opinion by Justice White.

Crawford v. Washington, decided March 8, 2004, held that where testimonial statements are at issue the only sufficient indicium of reliability is confrontation, so such statements of a witness who does not appear are inadmissible unless the witness is unavailable and the defendant had a prior opportunity for cross-examination; statements made during police interrogation fall squarely within the testimonial class. Opinion by Justice Scalia.

Miranda v. Arizona, decided June 13, 1966, held that statements from custodial interrogation are inadmissible unless the prosecution demonstrates procedural safeguards effective to secure the Fifth Amendment privilege against self-incrimination, and specified warnings covering the right to silence, that statements may be used in court, the right to consult and have counsel present during interrogation, and appointed counsel for the indigent; questioning must cease if the person invokes silence or asks for a lawyer. Opinion by Chief Justice Warren. Miranda rests on the Fifth Amendment, not the Sixth.

In re Winship, 397 U.S. 358 (1970), held that the Due Process Clause protects the accused against conviction except upon proof beyond a reasonable doubt of every fact necessary to constitute the crime charged.

Weeks v. United States, decided February 24, 1914, held that federal courts could not retain for use as evidence a defendant's letters and papers seized from his home without a warrant where he made a seasonable pretrial application for their return; the Fourth Amendment's protection reaches all alike, whether accused of crime or not, and binds all entrusted with enforcing federal law. Opinion by Justice Day. Weeks bound federal officers only.

Silverthorne Lumber Co. v. United States, decided January 26, 1920, held that unlawfully obtained evidence shall not be used at all rather than merely be kept from the courtroom, while stating expressly that if knowledge of the facts is gained from an independent source they may be proved like any others. Opinion by Justice Holmes. This is the origin of both derivative-evidence exclusion and the independent source limit.

Mapp v. Ohio, decided June 19, 1961, held that all evidence obtained by searches and seizures violating the Federal Constitution is inadmissible in a state criminal trial, overruling Wolf v. Colorado, 338 U.S. 25, insofar as it held otherwise. Opinion by Justice Clark; Justice Black concurring. Authorship was verified directly in the opinion text.

Wong Sun v. United States, decided January 14, 1963, framed the derivative-evidence question as whether, granting the primary illegality, the challenged evidence was come at by exploitation of that illegality or instead by means sufficiently distinguishable to be purged of the primary taint - the attenuation test. Opinion by Justice Brennan.

Nix v. Williams, decided June 11, 1984, adopted the inevitable discovery exception: if the prosecution establishes by a preponderance of the evidence that the information ultimately or inevitably would have been discovered by lawful means, the evidence should be received, and the prosecution need not prove the absence of bad faith. The same opinion describes the independent source doctrine as admitting evidence discovered by means wholly independent of any constitutional violation. Opinion by Chief Justice Burger.

United States v. Leon, decided July 5, 1984, held that the exclusionary rule does not bar the prosecution's case-in-chief use of evidence obtained by officers acting in reasonable reliance on a warrant issued by a detached and neutral magistrate but ultimately found invalid, while preserving inquiry into knowing or reckless falsity in the affidavit and into a magistrate serving as a rubber stamp. Opinion by Justice White for a six-Justice majority; Brennan, J., dissenting, joined by Marshall, J.; Stevens, J., dissenting separately.

Leon treats the use of the fruits of a past unlawful search as working no new Fourth Amendment wrong and treats exclusion as a judicially created remedy whose application is resolved by weighing costs and benefits, which is the doctrinal basis for separating the question of a right's violation from the question of remedy.

The empirical question whether the exclusionary rule deters police misconduct was not settled in Leon: the Court quoted United States v. Janis, 428 U.S. 433, 452, n. 22, for the proposition that no empirical researcher, proponent or opponent of the rule, had established with any assurance whether the rule has a deterrent effect.

Justice Brennan, dissenting in Leon and joined by Justice Marshall, argued that the language of deterrence and cost-benefit analysis, used indiscriminately, can have a narcotic effect and creates an illusion of technical precision, and that the majority ignored the constitutional importance of what was at stake. The lesson presents this position alongside the majority's without endorsing either.

Herring v. United States, decided January 14, 2009, held the exclusionary rule inapplicable when police mistakes leading to an unlawful search result from isolated negligence attenuated from the search rather than systemic error or reckless disregard of constitutional requirements, restating that the rule is not an individual right and applies only where deterrence outweighs the cost of letting guilty and possibly dangerous defendants go free. Opinion by Chief Justice Roberts.

The Supreme Court has described the Eighth Amendment's three clauses together as placing parallel limitations on the power of those entrusted with the criminal-law function of government (Timbs, quoting Browning-Ferris Industries of Vt., Inc. v. Kelco Disposal, Inc., 492 U.S. 257, 263 (1989), quoting Ingraham v. Wright, 430 U.S. 651, 664 (1977)).

Mapp states the case for the exclusionary rule in its own terms: without the Weeks rule the assurance against unreasonable federal searches and seizures would be 'a form of words', valueless and undeserving of mention in a perpetual charter of liberties - the phrase 'a form of words' being taken from Justice Holmes in Silverthorne.

Nix v. Williams states, in the body of the opinion and not only the syllabus, that significant disincentives to obtaining evidence illegally - including the possibility of departmental discipline and civil liability - lessen the likelihood that the inevitable discovery exception will promote police misconduct, which is the Court's own acknowledgement that remedies other than exclusion exist.

The McDonald footnote's catalogue is stated as covering the remaining unincorporated guarantees apart from the right at issue in that case and a separate question about Sixth Amendment jury unanimity; the lesson reproduces that qualification rather than presenting the four-item list as exhaustive.

In a U.S. criminal case the government carries the burden of proof, defendants who cannot afford counsel are advised of the right to a court-appointed attorney, and a federal acquittal cannot be appealed or the same offense recharged because of the double jeopardy prohibition.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the exclusionary rule deters police misconduct enough to justify its costs.
positions: The Leon majority treats exclusion as a remedy whose application must be justified by deterrence, weighed against costs it describes as real: keeping reliable evidence from juries and letting some guilty defendants go free.

Justice Brennan, dissenting with Justice Marshall in Leon, argues that indiscriminate cost-benefit language has a narcotic effect, creates an illusion of technical precision, and understates the constitutional stakes.
The Leon majority itself quotes United States v. Janis for the point that no researcher on either side has established the rule's deterrent effect with assurance.
conflictingEvidence.resolution: Presented as an open disagreement inside the U.S. Reports. The lesson states both positions, flags the empirical uncertainty the majority itself acknowledged, and takes no side, in keeping with the subject's politically-sensitive review profile.

conflictingEvidence.issue: Whether the Eighth Amendment's excessive bail prohibition binds the states.
positions: McDonald v. Chicago's footnote cites Schilb v. Kuebel, 404 U.S. 357 (1971), as only assuming that the excessive bail prohibition applies to the states.
The excessive fines clause was squarely incorporated only in Timbs v. Indiana (2019).
conflictingEvidence.resolution: The lesson does not assert that the excessive bail clause has been squarely incorporated. It states the Eighth Amendment's text, notes that Timbs incorporated the fines clause in 2019, and leaves bail practice to the pretrial topic.

The Supreme Court's own slip opinion for No. 17-1091 is retrievable and authoritative.

unsupportedExistingClaims: The generated draft's entire body was placeholder text with no legal content: it described 'constitutional protections' as a generic organizing concept, with vocabulary entries for 'context', 'evidence', and 'application' and a toolbox-drawer analogy. None of it stated anything about the Constitution and none of it was verifiable, so all of it was discarded.
The draft's three quick-check questions tested generic study skills rather than any constitutional content and carried no sources; they were replaced entirely.
The draft carried no sources at all and no jurisdictional statement, which a legal topic in this subject requires.
correctionsNeeded: Replaced the placeholder lesson with an amendment-by-amendment survey grounded in the constitutional text and in opinions read in the official United States Reports.
Added the explicit statement that this is educational material about U.S. federal constitutional law and not legal advice, and the note that state constitutions may protect more.

Added the incorporation history the draft omitted, including Barron v. Baltimore, Hurtado, the McDonald catalogue, and Timbs, because students commonly assume the Bill of Rights always bound the states.
Separated the question of a right's violation from the question of remedy, which the exclusionary-rule material depends on.

Verified opinion authorship directly in each opinion rather than relying on any summary, given documented misattribution by automated summarizers in this project. Confirmed: Marshall (Barron), Matthews (Hurtado), Day (Weeks), Holmes (Silverthorne), Clark (Mapp), Brennan (Wong Sun), Black (Gideon), Warren (Miranda), White (Duncan), Douglas (Argersinger), O'Connor (Strickland), Burger (Nix), White (Leon), Scalia (Crawford), Roberts (Herring), Alito (McDonald, Part II-D for the Court), Ginsburg (Timbs).
Kept Fourth Amendment doctrine at the level of text and structure so the later search-seizure-and-warrants topic owns it, and kept procedure out so the courts-unit topics own it.
rightsIssues: All constitutional text and all judicial opinions used are U.S. government edicts and are in the public domain; short doctrinal phrases from those opinions are quoted or closely tracked and are attributed to the deciding case.

Used for the Court's own catalogue, in footnote 13 of Part II-D of Justice Alito's opinion (Part II-D was joined by Roberts, C.J., and Scalia, Kennedy and Thomas, JJ., making it an opinion of the Court), of the guarantees not fully incorporated as of 2010: the Third Amendment's protection against quartering of soldiers, the Fifth Amendment's grand jury indictment requirement, the Seventh Amendment civil jury right, and the Eighth Amendment's prohibition on excessive fines. The accompanying footnote also records that Schilb v. Kuebel, 404 U.S. 357 (1971), only assumed the excessive bail prohibition applies to the states. Used to show that incorporation is selective and, read against Timbs (2019), to date the excessive fines holding precisely.

sourceRecords.notes: Official slip opinion downloaded and read; the bound-volume PDF for volume 586 was not retrievable from govinfo, so the Court's own slip opinion was used and the slip pagination is noted. Used for the holding that the Eighth Amendment's Excessive Fines Clause is an incorporated protection applicable to the states under the Fourteenth Amendment's Due Process Clause; for the incorporation standard (protections fundamental to our scheme of ordered liberty or deeply rooted in this Nation's history and tradition, quoting McDonald v. Chicago, 561 U.S. 742, 767); for the statement that once a protection is incorporated there is no daylight between the federal and state conduct it prohibits or requires; for the point that the inquiry asks whether the right guaranteed, not each particular application of it, is fundamental or deeply rooted; and for the facts (Indiana sought civil forfeiture of a Land Rover Timbs had bought for about $42,000, against a $10,000 maximum fine for his drug offense). Argued November 28, 2018; decided February 20, 2019. Lineup verified: Ginsburg, J., for the Court, joined by Roberts, C.J., and Breyer, Alito, Sotomayor, Kagan, Gorsuch and Kavanaugh, JJ.; Gorsuch, J., concurring; Thomas, J., concurring in the judgment.
